panels.title: Big questions
points: What makes a good person, according to these poets?
How do poets present what matters most to a community?
How do poets present identity and belonging?
How do poets present memory and childhood?

panels.title: Islamic foundation
panels.text: In Islam, water is a sign of Allah's mercy: 'We made from water every living thing' (al-Anbiya 21:30). Wasting it is discouraged even when it is plentiful. Dharker's title, Blessing, invites us to see water as a gift; note that the poem speaks of 'a kindly god' in its own setting.

panels.title: Prayer Before Birth (MacNeice): voice, plea and the threats of the world
points: Louis MacNeice, written in 1944
During the Second World War
Speaker: a child not yet born
Addressed to God and to humanity

panels.title: Blessing (Dharker): water, imagery and community
points: Imtiaz Dharker, born in Pakistan, raised in Glasgow
Set in a poor district of Mumbai, India
A municipal pipe bursts
The whole community rushes for water

panels.title: Search For My Tongue (Bhatt): language, identity and the extended metaphor
points: Sujata Bhatt, born 1956 in Ahmedabad, India
Moved to the USA as a child
First language: Gujarati
Overnight the mother tongue grows back

panels.title: Half-past Two (Fanthorpe) and Piano (Lawrence): childhood and memory
points: A boy told to stay 'till half-past two'
He cannot yet tell the time
Childish compounds: 'Gettinguptime', 'TVtime'
He slips into 'the clockless land of ever'

panels.title: Sonnet 116 (Shakespeare): constancy, form and the volta
points: Opens with negatives: love does not alter
'Love's not Time's fool'
Beauty fades with time's 'bending sickle'
Love lasts 'to the edge of doom'

panels.title: If- (Kipling): advice, the conditional and the closing promise
points: Rudyard Kipling (1865 to 1936)
Published 1910; addressed to 'my son'
A father's advice on how to become 'a Man'
Victorian and Edwardian ideals of self-control

panels.title: Hide and Seek (Scannell): second person, tension and the twist
points: Vernon Scannell (1922 to 2007)
The whole poem speaks to 'you', the hider
Imperatives: 'Call out', 'Hide in the shed'
We become the child

panels.title: Compare how memory is presented in Piano and Half-past Two.
points: P: both present memory as stronger than adult control, although one wounds and one delights
E: 'Betrays me back' / 'the clockless land of ever'
M: Lawrence's verb 'Betrays' versus Fanthorpe's invented phrase
A: memory overpowers Lawrence; it frees the boy
Answer: A fully integrated paragraph with both poems in every move.

panels.title: Introduction: Compare how the writers present childhood in Piano and Half-past Two.
points: Type and form: a lyric in couplets; a narrative poem in tercets
Author's purpose: mourn the past; celebrate a child's view
Perspective: an adult's grief; a child's wonder
Subject and question: both present childhood outside adult time

Answer: Piano, a lyric in rhyming couplets, mourns a lost childhood from an adult's grieving perspective, whereas Half-past Two, a narrative poem, celebrates a child's timeless wonder. Both poets present childhood as a world beyond adult time, but they feel very differently about it.
